summary: Specifies the NULL Authentication method and the ID_NULL identification type for IKEv2. It allows one-sided authentication or fully unauthenticated sessions when a peer cannot or will not authenticate.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes you only want a private chat without checking who is on the other end. This allows that.

questions: can ikev2 be used without authentication
subtitle: A way for an IKEv2 peer to skip authentication and identity, for anonymous or opportunistic encrypted sessions.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 gives no way for one or both peers to stay unauthenticated and anonymous, even though mutual authentication is sometimes undesirable, superfluous or impossible.
tldr.mechanism: It adds the NULL Authentication method and the ID_NULL identity type, both value 13, with an AUTH payload computed like a pre-shared secret from SK_pi or SK_pr and an empty identity.
tldr.outcome: Peers can run one-sided or fully unauthenticated IKE sessions, for example for opportunistic encryption against pervasive monitoring, as long as implementations keep such peers isolated and separate from authenticated ones.

facts.label: ID_NULL data
facts.value: Identification Data field MUST be empty

today: RFC 7619 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4301 (its PAD processing) and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Unauthenticated IKE
sections.content:
RFC 7619 extends IKEv2 (RFC 7296). Peers may use different authentication methods, but none lets a peer stay unauthenticated and anonymous. The RFC gives three cases.

  • A user wants an anonymous secure connection to a server: only the responder is authenticated.
  • A sensor wakes up and sends a measurement: the server authenticates the sensor, but the sensor does not need to authenticate the server.
  • Two peers with no trust relationship want protection against pervasive monitoring (RFC 7258) under Opportunistic Security (RFC 7435): the key exchange is fully unauthenticated.

In the last case an attacker willing to send packets can still mount a man-in-the-middle attack. The document therefore adds the NULL Authentication method and the ID_NULL ID type so a peer can say explicitly that it is unwilling or unable to certify its identity.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want a secret code with someone without showing ID, like whispering in a crowd. This gives IKE a way to do that on purpose.

sections.title: The NULL AUTH Payload
sections.content:
In IKEv2 each peer picks its own authentication method. A peer may use NULL authentication. If a host's local policy requires a non-null authenticated peer and it receives an AUTH payload with the NULL method, it MUST return AUTHENTICATION_FAILED. If an initiator uses EAP, the responder MUST NOT use NULL authentication.

An AUTH payload is still required, because it cryptographically links the IKE_SA_INIT messages to the rest of the IKE Security Association. Its content is computed with the pre-shared secret syntax of RFC 7296 Section 2.15, using SK_pi (initiator) or SK_pr (responder) as the secret, so the keys differ by direction. The authentication method value for NULL is 13.
sections.plainLanguage: You still seal the envelope so nobody can swap the letter, but you leave the name line blank.

sections.title: The ID_NULL Identity Type
sections.content:
If the remote peer is not authenticated, any ID it sends cannot be validated. To avoid sending a bogus ID with placeholder data, the RFC defines ID_NULL, whose Identification Data field MUST be empty. Its ID type value is 13.

When anonymity matters, ID_NULL SHOULD be used with NULL authentication. A real ID type may still be used for logging, troubleshooting, or when authentication happens out of band after the IKE SA is created. In any case the ID content MUST NOT be used for trust or policy checks in IKE_AUTH when NULL authentication is used. ID_NULL could also be used with other methods, such as raw public keys, but those uses belong in their own documents.
sections.plainLanguage: ID_NULL is a name tag left honestly empty, rather than one with a fake name written on it.

sections.title: Stale SAs and Traffic Selectors
sections.content:
An unauthenticated identity cannot find a peer's older IKE SAs, so INITIAL_CONTACT MUST NOT be used to delete other IKE SAs with the same identity without extra verification that they are stale. The normal Liveness Check of RFC 7296 can detect stale unauthenticated SAs, and creating a new one can trigger a check on existing ones. Implementations should weigh the cost of liveness checks against memory used by orphaned SAs.

Traffic Selectors are a second risk. A rogue peer could claim an address such as the DNS server 192.0.2.1 to receive traffic meant for others, especially behind NAT. Implementations SHOULD isolate anonymous peers from each other and from itself, for example by always assigning internal IP addresses, or by internal NAT and connection tracking. They MAY force single host-to-host SAs; with IPv6 they MUST be able to assign a full /64 block (RFC 5739) even to an unauthenticated peer.
sections.plainLanguage: If you cannot tell visitors apart by name, you must check whether old visitors have left. And you must not let a stranger say 'send me the mail for the whole house'.

sections.title: Changes to the PAD and SPD
sections.content:
The Peer Authorization Database (PAD) of RFC 4301 links the SPD to IKEv2. This RFC updates PAD processing: NULL authentication becomes a supported method with no authentication data, and ID_NULL joins the allowed ID types, with a matching rule that only checks the type, since there is no identity data.

Matching rules MUST include a new flag on each SPD entry saying whether unauthenticated peers may use it. Only entries with the flag explicitly on can serve unauthenticated connections, so authenticated and unauthenticated rules are kept apart. Appendix A lists the exact edits to Section 4.4.3 of RFC 4301.
sections.plainLanguage: The guest list gets a new rule: some rooms are marked 'strangers allowed', and strangers can only enter those.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Where authenticated IKE is possible for a Traffic Selector range, unauthenticated IKE SHOULD NOT be allowed for it. If both peers use NULL authentication, the whole exchange is open to active man-in-the-middle attacks. Using a non-null ID type with NULL authentication may expose the client's anonymity to such an attack.

Existing implementations assumed remote peers were identified, and those assumptions break. Logs of unproven IDs should be marked untrusted and probably include the remote IP, with rate limiting. Cookie-based DoS defenses do not distinguish a NULL-authenticated attacker, who is a fully legitimate IKE peer, so abusive Liveness probes or Delete requests become more likely.

An unauthenticated peer MUST NOT reach resources meant only for authenticated peers, or replace their Child SAs. Hosts MUST also pass decrypted traffic through the same packet filters as plaintext, since ESP (protocol 50) or ESPinUDP (UDP port 4500) packets would otherwise bypass them. IANA added value 13 to both the IKEv2 Authentication Method and ID Types registries.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody checks ID, anyone can pretend to be anyone, so the guests with no ID must be kept away from the private rooms, and watched carefully.
